addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

addedBlocks:
## npx
NotebookLM MCP - Access NotebookLM (notebooklm.google.com).

**Auth:** If you get authentication errors, run `nlm login` via your Bash/terminal tool. This is the automated authentication method that handles everything. Only use save_auth_tokens as a fallback if the CLI fails.
**Account Switching:** To switch Google Accounts for the MCP server, run `nlm login switch <profile>` in Bash. The MCP server instantly uses the active default profile.
**Confirmation:** Tools with confirm param require user approval before setting confirm=True.
**Studio:** After creating audio/video/infographic/slides, poll studio_status for completion.

Consolidated tools:
- source_add(source_type=url|text|drive|file, url=..., document_id=..., text=..., file_path=...): Add any source type
- studio_create(artifact_type=audio|video|...): Create any artifact type
- studio_revise: Revise individual slides in an existing slide deck
- download_artifact(artifact_type=audio|video|...): Download any artifact type
- note_create/note_list/note_update/note_delete: Manage notes in notebooks

attachment.content:
- skills: Reference codebase for Crates. Use this skill when you need to understand the structure, implementation patterns, or code details of the Crates project.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-app: This skill should be used when the user wants to build an "MCP app", add "interactive UI" or "widgets" to an MCP server, "render components in chat", build "MCP UI resources", make a tool that shows a "form", "picker", "dashboard" or "confirmation dialog" inline in the conversation, or mentions "apps SDK" in the context of MCP. Use AFTER the build-mcp-server skill has settled the deployment model, or when the user already knows they want UI widgets.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-server: This skill should be used when the user asks to "build an MCP server", "create an MCP", "make an MCP integration", "wrap an API for Claude", "expose tools to Claude", "make an MCP app", or discusses building something with the Model Context Protocol. It is the entry point for MCP server development — it interrogates the user about their use case, determines the right deployment model (remote HTTP, MCPB, local stdio), picks a tool-design pattern, and hands off to specialized skills.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcpb: This skill should be used when the user wants to "package an MCP server", "bundle an MCP", "make an MCPB", "ship a local MCP server", "distribute a local MCP", discusses ".mcpb files", mentions bundling a Node or Python runtime with their MCP server, or needs an MCP server that interacts with the local filesystem, desktop apps, or OS and must be installable without the user having Node/Python set up.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

| Tool | File | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **factory** | `~/.factory/mcp.json` | endpoint `100.90.37.1` → `10.220.35.1`; removed dead headerless `cognitive-mcp` http entry (`100.90.37.254:3003`) |

| **agy/antigravity** | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` | footprint `yqx3…`(bogus) → `antigravity`; added missing `GHOSTBRIDGE_TRACE_ID` |

## On the headers (your two questions)

**Correct headers** — settled by data, not guesswork. The shim maps `GHOSTBRIDGE_FOOTPRINT` → `x-ghostbridge-footprint` and `GHOSTBRIDGE_TRACE_ID` → `x-ghostbridge-trace-id`. Both should be the **client name**. The base64 footprints in the gemini/antigravity configs were bogus — they matched neither host WG pubkey (`XpO2…`, `iNqg…`) and were missing the trace-id entirely. Each client now sends a clean, distinct identity: `factory-droid`, `opencode`, `codex`, `gemini-cli`, `antigravity`.

**Endpoint** — I asked the cognitive server itself (healthy, `authStatus: chrome_profile`) and then probed the candidates. Only `10.220.35.1:50052` is OPEN — the one my own `.mcp.json` connection uses. `100.90.37.1`, `100.90.37.254:50052`, and the `:3003` HTTP gateway are all unreachable, despite still being referenced in `deploy/config/cognitive-mcp-clients.json`. That stale-config note and the header convention are now saved to memory.

**Context-aware code suggestions** — yes, but understand the shape: the shim reflects **18 `CognitiveToolService_*` tools** (verified through the live path) — `AskQuestion`, `QueryNotebook`, `ListNotebooks`, `GenerateDataTable`, `GeminiQuery`, etc. These are NotebookLM/RAG retrieval tools, not inline autocomplete. Context-awareness comes from the host agent *calling* `AskQuestion`/`QueryNotebook` to ground its suggestions in your notebooks/sources. That's why my earlier `AskQuestion` returned "no grounded answer" — the memory store currently holds only 2 entries / 2 namespaces, so suggestions are only as context-aware as the notebooks you've populated.

One thing I did **not** touch: `deploy/config/cognitive-mcp-clients.json` and `deploy/config/factory-mcp.json` still hardcode the stale `100.90.37.254` endpoints. Want me to update those deploy templates to `10.220.35.1` too, or are those tracking a different (future) gateway address?

content.text:
**No — it does not need to be called `VOYAGE_API_KEY`.** All three readers in the cognitive-mcp crate use the same precedence:

```rust
COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_KEY   // ← checked FIRST
  .or VOYAGE_API_KEY
  .or VOYAGE_API_KEY_RUST
```

(in `voyage.rs:43`, `rag_pipeline.rs:278`, and `qdrant_shuttle.rs:330`)

The s6 env file is already named `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_KEY` — the **highest-priority** name — so the `al-` key I put there is what the service uses, and it overrides any `VOYAGE_API_KEY` / `VOYAGE_API_KEY_RUST` in the environment. The name is correct; nothing else to rename.

Two related notes while I had the code open:

- **The `al-` key needs its endpoint set.** `qdrant_shuttle.rs:338` reads `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_URL` for the query-embedding URL. `al-`-prefixed keys are MongoDB-hosted (`https://ai.mongodb.com/v1/embeddings`) — `voyage.rs` auto-detects that from the `al-` prefix, but `qdrant_shuttle.rs` uses `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_URL` with a default. If that default is the public `api.voyageai.com`, the `al-` key will be rejected (401) at query time. Want me to check that default and add a `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_URL` env file pointing at the MongoDB endpoint?
- There's also `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_KEY_FILE` (`qdrant_shuttle.rs:395`) as an alternative to the inline key, if you'd rather reference a file than store the secret in the env dir.

## Where this leaves the Qdrant RAG

The key swap is done and the service is healthy, but it doesn't fix the bigger thing you flagged. Confirmed: the **gRPC reflection surface exposes only the 18 NotebookLM RPCs — zero code-RAG tools** (`code_search`/`code_context`/`code_index`). Those live in `code_tools.rs` and are only served over the **context HTTP surface**, which is gated by `server.rs:134` — and your env dir sets `COGNITIVE_MCP_CONTEXT_HTTP_DISABLED=1`, so that surface is **off**. Net: every client I just wired (all gRPC-shim) can reach NotebookLM but **cannot reach the Qdrant code-RAG**, because it's not on the gRPC surface and the HTTP surface is disabled.

To actually get Qdrant RAG to those clients, you'd pick one:
1. **Enable the context HTTP surface** (drop/zero `COGNITIVE_MCP_CONTEXT_HTTP_DISABLED`, bind `:3003`) and point clients at it instead of the gRPC shim — but that's an HTTP MCP endpoint, not the reflection shim.
2. **Expose code-RAG over gRPC** by adding `CodeSearch`/`CodeContext` RPCs to `cognitive.proto` so the shim reflects them — a code change.

Want me to verify the `al-` endpoint default first (quick, avoids a silent 401), and then dig into which of those two RAG-exposure paths fits your architecture?

If that default is the public `api.voyageai.com`, the `al-` key will 401 at query time and Qdrant RAG retrieval will silently fail even though the service is healthy. #!/bin/sh
# 🟢 🛷 Safely build, commit and activate the canonical Artix s6 service set.
#
# The s6 frontend generates the boot bundle during `s6 set commit`. Compiling
# /etc/s6/sv directly bypasses that step and can produce a database without the
# `default` runlevel, which makes the next boot fail in rc.init.
set -eu

PROJECT_ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)
S6_COMPILED_LINK=${S6_COMPILED_LINK:-/etc/s6/rc/compiled}
DEFAULT_BUNDLE=${DEFAULT_BUNDLE:-default}

# Build the Rust workspace as the unprivileged user who owns the source tree,
# then install every binary target to /usr/local/bin. This keeps the cargo
# cache and target directory owned by the developer while allowing the final
# install and s6 activation to run as root.
BUILD_USER=${BUILD_USER:-$(logname 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' "${SUDO_USER:-$USER}")}

build_workspace() {
    echo "Building workspace binaries as $BUILD_USER..."
    cd "$PROJECT_ROOT"
    sudo -u "$BUILD_USER" cargo build --workspace --release
}

install_binaries() {
    echo "Installing built binaries to /usr/local/bin..."
    cd "$PROJECT_ROOT"
    find target/release -maxdepth 1 -type f -executable -print0 |
        while IFS= read -r -d '' bin; do
            install -Dm755 "$bin" "/usr/local/bin/$(basename "$bin")"
        done
}

if ! command -v s6 >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! command -v s6-rc-db >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "s6 frontend or s6-rc-db not found" >&2
    exit 127
fi

if [ "${SKIP_BUILD:-}" != "1" ]; then
    build_workspace
fi
install_binaries

old_db="$(readlink -f "$S6_COMPILED_LINK" 2>/dev/null || true)"

echo "Synchronizing the canonical s6 repository"
s6 repository sync
s6 set check -F -u
s6 set commit -f -D "$DEFAULT_BUNDLE"

new_db="$(readlink -f /etc/s6/repo/compiled/current)"
if [ -z "$new_db" ] || [ ! -f "$new_db/db" ]; then
    echo "s6 frontend did not produce a compiled database" >&2
    exit 1
fi

s6-rc-db -c "$new_db" check
if ! s6-rc-db -c "$new_db" list bundles | grep -Fxq "$DEFAULT_BUNDLE"; then
    echo "refusing unsafe database: missing boot bundle '$DEFAULT_BUNDLE'" >&2
    exit 1
fi

echo "Updating live s6-rc state to: $new_db"
if ! s6 live install -b; then
    echo "s6 live install failed; leaving $S6_COMPILED_LINK unchanged" >&2
    [ -n "$old_db" ] && echo "current compiled DB remains: $old_db" >&2
    exit 1
fi

ln -sfnT "$new_db" "$S6_COMPILED_LINK"
if [ "$(readlink -f "$S6_COMPILED_LINK")" != "$new_db" ]; then
    echo "failed to point bootdb at the committed database" >&2
    exit 1
fi

echo "Activated s6-rc database: $new_db"

content.text:
Critical — this changes the reboot calculus. The wedge is **`op-web-srv`**:

```
298  s6-rc -up change default
 └─ 626  s6-svlisten -U -- .../op-web-srv   s6-svc -u -- .../op-web-srv
```

`s6-rc -up change default` is stuck waiting (`s6-svlisten -U` = wait-until-up) for **`op-web-srv`** to signal readiness, which it never does — so the whole boot transition hangs and holds the global lock. This matches SIGNALS.md ("op-web :8080 — nothing listening"). **A reboot will re-wedge identically** unless `op-web-srv` is fixed. Let me confirm its readiness setup:

content.text:
Now the picture is complete. `op-web-srv` is a **longrun with `notification-fd = 3`** (s6 waits for a readiness notification on fd 3). The process is alive (pid 4290, 60 min) but **never bound :8080 and never sent the readiness signal** — so `s6-svlisten -U` waits forever. It's stuck in its own init, most likely blocked reaching `OP_DBUS_GRPC_ADDR=http://10.200.0.1:50051` or the dbus session bus. This is the SIGNALS.md OD-23 "op-web :8080 down" issue.

The good news for your reboot decision: op-cognitive-mcp **is currently up from this same wedged transaction**, which proves it comes up *independently of* op-web-srv. Let me confirm there's no dependency edge, so I can tell you definitively whether the reboot applies your change:

2	name: artix-s6-layout
3	description: "Artix Linux s6 service layout — exact structure for adding services, canonical deploy script"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: 530852a9-02e8-4af8-bdf1-8d45b02180a7
8	---
9	
10	# Artix Linux S6 Layout
11	
12	This host runs **Artix Linux** with s6-rc. Service sources live in `/etc/s6/sv/`, compiled DB at `/etc/s6/rc/compiled`.
13	
14	## Canonical workflow for adding a new service
15	
16	### 1. Create source files in the deploy tree (git-tracked)
17	
18	```
19	deploy/s6/op-<name>-srv/
20	  run              — executable sh script, use `exec s6-setuidgid jeremy /usr/local/bin/<binary>`
21	  type             — contains "longrun"
22	  notification-fd  — contains "3"
23	  producer-for     — contains "op-<name>-log"
24	  dependencies.d/
25	    dbus-session   — empty file (dependency)
26	    op-cognitive-mcp — empty file (if needs memory)
27	
28	deploy/s6/op-<name>-log/
29	  run              — execlineb logger script (see template below)
30	  type             — contains "longrun"
31	  notification-fd  — contains "3"
32	  consumer-for     — contains "op-<name>-srv"
33	  pipeline-name    — contains "op-<name>"
34	```
35	
36	### 2. Logger run script template (execlineb)
37	
38	```
39	#!/bin/execlineb -P
40	envfile -I /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf
41	importas -sCuD "n5 s2000000 T" DIRECTIVES DIRECTIVES
42	ifelse { test -w /var/log } {
43		foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /var/log/op-<name> }
44		s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /var/log/op-<name>
45	}
46	foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /run/log/op-<name> }
47	s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /run/log/op-<name>
48	```
49	
50	Requires an empty conf file: `sudo touch /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf`
51	
52	### 3. Copy to live system
53	
54	```bash
55	sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-srv /etc/s6/sv/
56	sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-log /etc/s6/sv/
57	```
58	
59	### 4. Register in the s6 frontend source tree
60	
61	New services need symlinks in the `active/` and `usable/` source directories:
62	
63	```bash
64	for svc in op-<name>-srv op-<name>-log; do
65	  sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/${svc}" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/${svc}"
66	done
67	sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/op-<name>-srv" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/op-<name>-srv"
68	```
69	
70	Also add to a bundle's `contents.d/`:
71	```bash
72	sudo touch /etc/s6/sv/misc/contents.d/op-<name>-srv
73	```
74	
75	### 5. Compile and install (when .ref rebuild works)
76	
77	```bash
78	sudo s6 set commit --default-bundle=system-default
79	sudo s6 live install
80	sudo s6 live start op-<name>-srv
81	```
82	
83	**Current blocker:** `s6 set commit` fails with `rpcbind-srv is not a valid identifier in .ref` when adding services not yet in the compiled `.ref` database. The `.ref` at `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` needs a full rebuild. Workaround: add startup to `rc-local/up`.
84	
85	## Enable an EXISTING service for boot (persistence)
86	
87	If `s6 set status` shows a service as `<name>/usable` (available but NOT enabled), it is absent from the `default` boot bundle and won't auto-start. To make it persistent:
88	
89	```bash
90	sudo s6 set enable op-<name>          # usable -> active in working set
91	sudo sh deploy/s6/recompile-and-update.sh   # commits + s6 live install, preserves `default` bundle
92	sudo s6 live start op-<name>          # live install resets servicedir; start it now
93	```
94	
95	Verify: `s6-rc-db -c /run/s6-rc/compiled all-dependencies default | grep op-<name>` (in boot tree), and `s6-svstat` shows `up` WITHOUT "normally down" (the "normally down" suffix means a stale `down` flag / not enabled). `recompile-and-update.sh` worked cleanly on 2026-06-19 — it's the canonical commit+install path; do NOT hand-run `s6 set commit`/`s6-rc-db` directly.
96	
97	## Key paths
98	
99	| Path | Purpose |
100	|------|---------|
101	| `/etc/s6/sv/` | Live service source definitions (= `.atomics/` symlink target) |
102	| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/current` | Active compiled s6-rc DB |
103	| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` | Working-set reference DB (separate from live) |
104	| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/` | Symlinks to services included in compilation |
105	| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/` | Symlinks to services enabled at boot |
106	| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0000/` | Store 0 = mirrors `/etc/s6/sv/` service dirs |
107	| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0001/` | Store 1 = extra services (mount-filesystems, network) |
108	| `/etc/s6/config/*.conf` | Logger directive files (can be empty) |
109	
110	## Do NOT use
111	
112	- `s6 set commit` without `--default-bundle` — fails with "bundle default already defined"
113	- Manual symlinks into `/run/service/` — wrong approach, s6-svscan manages that
114	- `pipeline-name` file value must NOT match the service directory name — causes duplicate definition compile error
115	
116	## Environment variables in run scripts
117	
118	Use `export VAR="${VAR:-default}"` pattern. For secrets, use `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/` directory (one file per variable, filename = var name, file content = value), accessed via `exec s6-envdir ./env ...` or `s6-setuidgid`.

# Artix Linux S6 Layout

This host runs **Artix Linux** with s6-rc. Service sources live in `/etc/s6/sv/`, compiled DB at `/etc/s6/rc/compiled`.

## Canonical workflow for adding a new service

### 1. Create source files in the deploy tree (git-tracked)

```
deploy/s6/op-<name>-srv/
  run              — executable sh script, use `exec s6-setuidgid jeremy /usr/local/bin/<binary>`
  type             — contains "longrun"
  notification-fd  — contains "3"
  producer-for     — contains "op-<name>-log"
  dependencies.d/
    dbus-session   — empty file (dependency)
    op-cognitive-mcp — empty file (if needs memory)

deploy/s6/op-<name>-log/
  run              — execlineb logger script (see template below)
  type             — contains "longrun"
  notification-fd  — contains "3"
  consumer-for     — contains "op-<name>-srv"
  pipeline-name    — contains "op-<name>"
```

### 2. Logger run script template (execlineb)

```
#!/bin/execlineb -P
envfile -I /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf
importas -sCuD "n5 s2000000 T" DIRECTIVES DIRECTIVES
ifelse { test -w /var/log } {
	foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /var/log/op-<name> }
	s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /var/log/op-<name>
}
foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /run/log/op-<name> }
s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /run/log/op-<name>
```

Requires an empty conf file: `sudo touch /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf`

### 3. Copy to live system

```bash
sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-srv /etc/s6/sv/
sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-log /etc/s6/sv/
```

### 4. Register in the s6 frontend source tree

New services need symlinks in the `active/` and `usable/` source directories:

```bash
for svc in op-<name>-srv op-<name>-log; do
  sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/${svc}" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/${svc}"
done
sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/op-<name>-srv" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/op-<name>-srv"
```

Also add to a bundle's `contents.d/`:
```bash
sudo touch /etc/s6/sv/misc/contents.d/op-<name>-srv
```

### 5. Compile and install (when .ref rebuild works)

```bash
sudo s6 set commit --default-bundle=system-default
sudo s6 live install
sudo s6 live start op-<name>-srv
```

**Current blocker:** `s6 set commit` fails with `rpcbind-srv is not a valid identifier in .ref` when adding services not yet in the compiled `.ref` database. The `.ref` at `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` needs a full rebuild. Workaround: add startup to `rc-local/up`.

## Enable an EXISTING service for boot (persistence)

If `s6 set status` shows a service as `<name>/usable` (available but NOT enabled), it is absent from the `default` boot bundle and won't auto-start. To make it persistent:

```bash
sudo s6 set enable op-<name>          # usable -> active in working set
sudo sh deploy/s6/recompile-and-update.sh   # commits + s6 live install, preserves `default` bundle
sudo s6 live start op-<name>          # live install resets servicedir; start it now
```

Verify: `s6-rc-db -c /run/s6-rc/compiled all-dependencies default | grep op-<name>` (in boot tree), and `s6-svstat` shows `up` WITHOUT "normally down" (the "normally down" suffix means a stale `down` flag / not enabled). `recompile-and-update.sh` worked cleanly on 2026-06-19 — it's the canonical commit+install path; do NOT hand-run `s6 set commit`/`s6-rc-db` directly.

## Key paths

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/etc/s6/sv/` | Live service source definitions (= `.atomics/` symlink target) |
| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/current` | Active compiled s6-rc DB |
| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` | Working-set reference DB (separate from live) |
| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/` | Symlinks to services included in compilation |
| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/` | Symlinks to services enabled at boot |
| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0000/` | Store 0 = mirrors `/etc/s6/sv/` service dirs |
| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0001/` | Store 1 = extra services (mount-filesystems, network) |
| `/etc/s6/config/*.conf` | Logger directive files (can be empty) |

## Do NOT use

- `s6 set commit` without `--default-bundle` — fails with "bundle default already defined"
- Manual symlinks into `/run/service/` — wrong approach, s6-svscan manages that
- `pipeline-name` file value must NOT match the service directory name — causes duplicate definition compile error

## Environment variables in run scripts

Use `export VAR="${VAR:-default}"` pattern. For secrets, use `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/` directory (one file per variable, filename = var name, file content = value), accessed via `exec s6-envdir ./env ...` or `s6-setuidgid`.

## Changing an existing service's env (e.g. a key in `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/`)

Editing `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/VAR` then `s6-svc -r` does **NOT** apply it: the run script does `s6-envdir ./env` relative to the **live** servicedir `/run/s6-rc/servicedirs/<name>` (a frozen copy installed at boot, tmpfs), not `/etc/s6/sv`. You must recompile→install:
```bash
sudo s6 repository sync          # pull /etc/s6/sv edits into repo sources
sudo s6 set check -F -u
sudo s6 set commit -f -D default # -D default = avoids "bundle default already defined"
new_db="$(sudo readlink -f /etc/s6/repo/compiled/current)"
sudo s6 live install -b          # swaps live servicedirs (regenerated from source)
sudo ln -sfnT "$new_db" /etc/s6/rc/compiled   # repoint bootdb for REBOOT persistence
```
This is exactly what `deploy/s6/recompile-and-update.sh` automates (run with `SKIP_BUILD=1` to skip the cargo rebuild for env-only changes). `/etc/s6/sv` = persistent source; `/etc/s6/rc/compiled` symlink = what boot loads; `/run/s6-rc` = live tmpfs copy.

## BOOT WEDGE: `op-web-srv` holds the global s6-rc lock (2026-06-20)

`op-web-srv` is a `longrun` with `notification-fd=3` (s6 waits for a readiness notify). `op-web-server` starts but never binds `:8080` and never notifies ready (stuck in init — likely can't reach `OP_DBUS_GRPC_ADDR=http://10.200.0.1:50051` or dbus-session). So at boot `s6-rc -up change default` (pid ~298) blocks forever on `s6-svlisten -U -- op-web-srv`, **holding the global s6-rc lock**. Effect: every `s6 live install` / `s6-rc-update` **hangs** (use a `timeout`; don't trust `-b`). Unrelated services still come up — op-cognitive-mcp (deps: only `dbus-session`, no readiness gate) is up despite the wedge — so a **reboot DOES apply servicedir/env changes** to such services; it just re-wedges the lock again until op-web is fixed (readiness or remove notification-fd). This is SIGNALS OD-23. Do NOT force-kill pid 298 lightly (global lock → cascade risk; cf. [[project_incus_boot_wedge]]). See [[project_cognitive_grpc_endpoint]].

content.text:
Root cause is now unambiguous: **op-web-server has no s6 readiness support at all** — there's no `sd_notify`/fd-3 write anywhere in `crates/op-web/src`. But the service declares `notification-fd=3`, so s6 blocks the boot transition forever waiting for a readiness byte that the binary is never going to send. (Separately it also can't reach its gRPC backend at `10.200.0.1:50051` and logs DBus/transport WARNs, but those are non-fatal retries.)

So the fix is to **remove the bogus `notification-fd` readiness gate** — then s6 marks op-web-srv "up" as soon as it execs, the boot transition completes, the lock releases, and op-web can keep retrying `:8080` in the background without wedging anything. And `s6 set commit` (compile) works even with the lock held — only live-install is blocked — so I can stage this for a clean reboot. Let me check the git-tracked source too:

That's the trap I suspected — fixing op-web alone would just relocate the wedge:

- **dbus-srv**: `up, ready` ✓ (genuinely supports readiness — leave it)
- **op-web-srv**: `up, normally down` (never notified — the current wedge)
- **op-assistant-grpc-srv**: `down (not started yet)` — the transaction hasn't even reached it, and it **also** has `notification-fd=3` with **no readiness support** in the binary. Once op-web is fixed, the boot transition would advance and **wedge here instead**.

# Artix Linux S6 Layout

This host runs **Artix Linux** with s6-rc. Service sources live in `/etc/s6/sv/`, compiled DB at `/etc/s6/rc/compiled`.

## Canonical workflow for adding a new service

### 1. Create source files in the deploy tree (git-tracked)

### 2. Logger run script template (execlineb)

```
#!/bin/execlineb -P
envfile -I /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf
importas -sCuD "n5 s2000000 T" DIRECTIVES DIRECTIVES
ifelse { test -w /var/log } {
	foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /var/log/op-<name> }
	s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /var/log/op-<name>
}
foreground { install -d -o s6log -g s6log /run/log/op-<name> }
s6-setuidgid s6log exec -c s6-log -d3 -b -- ${DIRECTIVES} /run/log/op-<name>
```

Requires an empty conf file: `sudo touch /etc/s6/config/op-<name>.conf`

### 3. Copy to live system

```bash
sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-srv /etc/s6/sv/
sudo cp -r deploy/s6/op-<name>-log /etc/s6/sv/
```

### 4. Register in the s6 frontend source tree

New services need symlinks in the `active/` and `usable/` source directories:

```bash
for svc in op-<name>-srv op-<name>-log; do
  sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/${svc}" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/${svc}"
done
sudo ln -sf "../../.atomics/op-<name>-srv" "/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/op-<name>-srv"
```

Also add to a bundle's `contents.d/`:
```bash
sudo touch /etc/s6/sv/misc/contents.d/op-<name>-srv
```

### 5. Compile and install (when .ref rebuild works)

```bash
sudo s6 set commit --default-bundle=system-default
sudo s6 live install
sudo s6 live start op-<name>-srv
```

**Current blocker:** `s6 set commit` fails with `rpcbind-srv is not a valid identifier in .ref` when adding services not yet in the compiled `.ref` database. The `.ref` at `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` needs a full rebuild. Workaround: add startup to `rc-local/up`.

## Enable an EXISTING service for boot (persistence)

If `s6 set status` shows a service as `<name>/usable` (available but NOT enabled), it is absent from the `default` boot bundle and won't auto-start. To make it persistent:

```bash
sudo s6 set enable op-<name>          # usable -> active in working set
sudo sh deploy/s6/recompile-and-update.sh   # commits + s6 live install, preserves `default` bundle
sudo s6 live start op-<name>          # live install resets servicedir; start it now
```

Verify: `s6-rc-db -c /run/s6-rc/compiled all-dependencies default | grep op-<name>` (in boot tree), and `s6-svstat` shows `up` WITHOUT "normally down" (the "normally down" suffix means a stale `down` flag / not enabled). `recompile-and-update.sh` worked cleanly on 2026-06-19 — it's the canonical commit+install path; do NOT hand-run `s6 set commit`/`s6-rc-db` directly.

## Changing an existing service's env (e.g. a key in `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/`)

Editing `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/VAR` then `s6-svc -r` does **NOT** apply it: the run script does `s6-envdir ./env` relative to the **live** servicedir `/run/s6-rc/servicedirs/<name>` (a frozen copy installed at boot, tmpfs), not `/etc/s6/sv`. You must recompile→install:
```bash
sudo s6 repository sync          # pull /etc/s6/sv edits into repo sources
sudo s6 set check -F -u
sudo s6 set commit -f -D default # -D default = avoids "bundle default already defined"
new_db="$(sudo readlink -f /etc/s6/repo/compiled/current)"
sudo s6 live install -b          # swaps live servicedirs (regenerated from source)
sudo ln -sfnT "$new_db" /etc/s6/rc/compiled   # repoint bootdb for REBOOT persistence
```
This is exactly what `deploy/s6/recompile-and-update.sh` automates (run with `SKIP_BUILD=1` to skip the cargo rebuild for env-only changes). `/etc/s6/sv` = persistent source; `/etc/s6/rc/compiled` symlink = what boot loads; `/run/s6-rc` = live tmpfs copy.

## BOOT WEDGE: `op-web-srv` holds the global s6-rc lock (2026-06-20)

`op-web-srv` is a `longrun` with `notification-fd=3` (s6 waits for a readiness notify). `op-web-server` starts but never binds `:8080` and never notifies ready (stuck in init — likely can't reach `OP_DBUS_GRPC_ADDR=http://10.200.0.1:50051` or dbus-session). So at boot `s6-rc -up change default` (pid ~298) blocks forever on `s6-svlisten -U -- op-web-srv`, **holding the global s6-rc lock**. Effect: every `s6 live install` / `s6-rc-update` **hangs** (use a `timeout`; don't trust `-b`). Unrelated services still come up — op-cognitive-mcp (deps: only `dbus-session`, no readiness gate) is up despite the wedge — so a **reboot DOES apply servicedir/env changes** to such services; it just re-wedges the lock again until op-web is fixed (readiness or remove notification-fd). This is SIGNALS OD-23. Do NOT force-kill pid 298 lightly (global lock → cascade risk; cf. [[project_incus_boot_wedge]]). See [[project_cognitive_grpc_endpoint]].

## Key paths

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/etc/s6/sv/` | Live service source definitions (= `.atomics/` symlink target) |
| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/current` | Active compiled s6-rc DB |
| `/etc/s6/repo/compiled/.ref` | Working-set reference DB (separate from live) |
| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/active/` | Symlinks to services included in compilation |
| `/etc/s6/repo/sources/current/usable/` | Symlinks to services enabled at boot |
| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0000/` | Store 0 = mirrors `/etc/s6/sv/` service dirs |
| `/etc/s6/repo/stores/0001/` | Store 1 = extra services (mount-filesystems, network) |
| `/etc/s6/config/*.conf` | Logger directive files (can be empty) |

## Do NOT use

- `s6 set commit` without `--default-bundle` — fails with "bundle default already defined"
- Manual symlinks into `/run/service/` — wrong approach, s6-svscan manages that
- `pipeline-name` file value must NOT match the service directory name — causes duplicate definition compile error

## Environment variables in run scripts

Use `export VAR="${VAR:-default}"` pattern. For secrets, use `/etc/s6/sv/<name>/env/` directory (one file per variable, filename = var name, file content = value), accessed via `exec s6-envdir ./env ...` or `s6-setuidgid`.

## What I fixed
The wedge wasn't really "op-web" — it was a **misconfigured s6 readiness gate**. `op-web-srv` (and `op-assistant-grpc-srv`) declared `notification-fd=3`, telling s6 to block the boot transition until the binary writes a readiness byte to fd 3 — but **neither Rust binary implements s6 readiness at all**, so `s6-svlisten -U` waited forever, holding the global s6-rc lock for the whole uptime.

Removed the bogus `notification-fd` from **both** services (live store `/etc/s6/sv/` + git source `deploy/s6/`), recompiled, and repointed the bootdb. I caught op-assistant too because the transaction hadn't reached it yet — fixing op-web alone would have just relocated the wedge to it on the next boot. `dbus-srv` genuinely signals `ready`, so I left its gate intact.

## Next reboot will now be clean
1. Live servicedirs install from the new bootdb (op-cognitive-mcp = `al-` key + ctx-http `0`).
2. `s6-rc -up change default` brings up op-web-srv / op-assistant-grpc-srv — now marked **up immediately on exec** (no readiness wait) → **transaction completes, lock releases, no wedge**.
3. op-cognitive-mcp comes up with the `al-` key and context-HTTP/tonic-web live on `:3003`.

op-web still won't *serve* `:8080` until its gRPC backend (`10.200.0.1:50051`) is reachable — but that's a runtime issue that no longer blocks boot or holds the lock.

The user-facing `createsocket` adds that declaration and wires the D-Bus socket controller / passthrough. Checked the code — **no, `--name` does not create a namespace.** In the current `openflow.rs`, `create_socket_port` (lines 536–553) does exactly two things with the name:

```rust
self.ovsdb_client.add_port(bridge, &port.name).await?;            // add OVS port named <name>
self.ovsdb_client.set_interface_type(&port.name, "internal").await?;  // make it an OVS internal port
```

So `--name <name>` creates an **OVS internal port** on the bridge (type `internal`) — not a network namespace. There's no `ip netns add`, no `setns`, no netns move anywhere in this path. And `SocketPort` only knows two types: `Privacy` (gbr_wg/xray/warp) and `SharedIngress` (`{bridge}-sock`) — both host-side OVS ports, no per-container ns concept.

That said, an OVS **internal port is the building block** for a container ns: you create the internal port, then `ip link set <name> netns <container>` moves it into the container's namespace. The current code does step 1 but **not** the netns move — so the "ns for routing" part isn't implemented; the name just becomes a host-side OVS internal port today.

So if the intent is "`--name` = the container's ns," that's the gap: `create_socket_port` would need to (a) create the OVS internal port and (b) push it into the named container's network namespace. Right now it stops at (a).

Want me to confirm whether anything *else* in the tree does the netns move (e.g. the OVS daemon or a container-provisioning step), before we conclude the per-container ns is genuinely unimplemented?

content.text:
Good questions — and they're really one question: **does `--name` need to be a network namespace?** With a shared `container.sock`, my honest answer is **no, that's overkill — and it's a category mismatch.**

Here's the technical reason:

**Filesystem unix sockets are not scoped by network namespace.** `container.sock` is a path (`/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`), and the plugin binds it with `UnixListener::bind(path)`. A path-based UDS lives in the **filesystem/mount** namespace and is reachable by anyone who can see the path — the **network** namespace is irrelevant to it. (Only *abstract* `@`-sockets are netns-scoped, and you're not using those.) So putting a shared UDS "in a namespace" doesn't isolate or route anything — you'd just be bind-mounting the same socket into each container's mount ns anyway. For the shared socket, `--name` should be a **routing/identity tag** that the bridge/xray demuxes on, not a netns.

**Where ns *does* buy you functionality + stability:** the **IP ingress plane** — xray domain-routing straight to a container's *network stack*. That's a container with its own netns + an OVS internal port moved into it (the `openflow.rs` path). There, ns gives you real isolation, independent routing tables, and per-container teardown without touching others. But that plane is about IP/TCP to the container, **not** the shared UDS to tonic-web. Two different planes:

| Plane | Transport | Does ns help? |
|---|---|---|
| Container → tonic-web | shared `container.sock` (UDS) | **No** — UDS isn't netns-scoped; `--name` = demux tag |
| xray → container service | IP/TCP to container | **Yes** — OVS internal port + netns (openflow's job) |

So my recommendation: **`createunixsocket --name --port` in the unix-socket plugin stays simple** — it declares/binds the shared `container.sock` and registers `--name` as the identity/demux tag. No netns in this method. And on "I don't want a thousand ports": you don't need them — with gRPC-over-UDS the bridge demuxes by **service/method via reflection**, so `--name` (tag) is enough; `--port` only matters as metadata if a backend is *non-gRPC* (raw TCP) and the bridge must map tag→port. Keep ns where it earns its keep: the openflow/OVS IP plane, as a separate concern.

Net: `--name` = tag, not namespace. Want me to implement `createunixsocket` in the unix-socket plugin on that basis (shared socket + name-as-tag, ports optional metadata)?

content.text:
You're right — I overgeneralized (the thing you've told me not to do). **Ports are not unnecessary.** tonic-web auto-demux only works for **gRPC** traffic — it demuxes by gRPC service/method. A mail container speaks **raw TCP** (SMTP 25/465/587, IMAP 143/993, POP 110/995) — none of that is gRPC, so there's nothing for tonic-web to demux on. For those, the ports are essential.

So the honest split:

| Backend type | Demux mechanism | `--port` needed? |
|---|---|---|
| gRPC service (over the shared socket) | tonic-web by service/method (reflection) | No — optional metadata |
| Raw TCP, single protocol | by name/SNI | Maybe (one port) |
| **Raw TCP, multi-port (mail, etc.)** | by **port** — gRPC demux can't apply | **Yes — required** |

So `--port <list>` stays in the signature exactly as you had it (`--name <name> --port 1,2,3,4,5`). For a mail container, `--name mail --port 25,465,587,143,993,110,995` records the ports the container serves, because the routing layer (xray by domain+port, or the bridge's port-aware passthrough) has to know them — there's no gRPC method name to route on.

My earlier "ports unnecessary" only held for the pure-gRPC case; it breaks the moment a container is non-gRPC or multi-protocol like mail. Corrected model:

- **`--name`** = identity/demux tag (not a namespace — UDS still isn't netns-scoped).
- **`--port <list>`** = the TCP ports that container exposes; required for non-gRPC/multi-port (mail), optional for pure-gRPC where tonic-web auto-demuxes.
- Lives in the **unix-socket plugin**, shared `container.sock`.

Does that match how you're thinking about mail — `--port` carries the real protocol ports for non-gRPC containers, and gRPC ones can omit it?

content.text:
Good question to stop on — let me answer it straight from the code, because the answer is **no, xray does not use OpenFlow. They're two separate layers that gemma configures independently.**

Here's what the code actually shows:

- **gemma generates both** — `main.rs` builds one `XrayRoutingMap { xray_routes, openflow_rules }` and writes **two separate artifacts**: the xray config *and* the OpenFlow rules. So gemma feeds both, but they're consumed by different components. (That dual output is probably the source of the confusion.)

- **OpenFlow/OVS = L2/L3 packet steering + obfuscation.** `openflow.rs` manages flows for the privacy chain `gbr_wg → gbr_warp → gbr_xray` and the obfuscation levels. It steers packets across bridge ports — including *into* the `gbr_xray` port. It works on match-fields (in_port, dl_type, nw_dst/tp_dst), not domains.

- **xray = L7 SNI/domain routing.** xray sits at the `gbr_xray` port and routes by **SNI/domain/identity** to backends (container ns, or `container.sock` → tonic-web). It has no idea OpenFlow exists.

So the relationship is a stack, not a dependency:

```
WG ingress → [OVS/OpenFlow: gbr_wg → gbr_warp → gbr_xray + obfuscation]  ← openflow_rules (gemma)
                                        ↓ (packets handed to the xray port)
                              [xray: SNI/domain routing]                  ← xray config.json (gemma)
                                        ↓
                        container ns  /  container.sock → tonic-web
```

OpenFlow gets traffic *to* xray and does the privacy/obfuscation; xray does the application-layer routing. Neither calls the other — gemma is the common brain that emits config for both.

Let me ground this in what the code actually does, because "OSCAL tag routing = OpenFlow" isn't quite what's built — and that determines whether `createunixsocket` needs OVS.

**What gemma's OpenFlow generation actually matches on** (`main.rs` `backend_to_openflow_rule`):
- TCP/GRPC backends → an OpenFlow rule matching `dl_type` + `nw_proto` + **`nw_dst` + `tp_dst`** (IP + TCP port) → `output:ovsbr0-mgmt`.
- **Unix-socket backends → returns `None`** (no OpenFlow rule) — the code comment says they "route through the tonic-web gRPC bridge (reflection demuxes) so no OVS bridge match is needed."

So as-built, OpenFlow does **IP/port matching + the privacy chain** (gbr_wg→warp→xray + obfuscation). The **OSCAL subids are route *metadata*, not OVS match fields** — nothing in OpenFlow matches on a subid tag string. (OpenFlow physically can't match a string; it matches packet fields — so "tag routing in OpenFlow" would require encoding the subid into a VLAN/metadata register/port first, which isn't built.)

So there are two real models, and your instinct is pointing at the second:

| Model | Tag routing happens at | Does createunixsocket need OVS? |
|---|---|---|
| **As-built** | Unix sockets bypass OpenFlow; **tonic-web demuxes by reflection**; OSCAL subid is just gemma/xray metadata | **No** — pure UDS |
| **OpenFlow tag routing** (your instinct) | OSCAL subid encoded as an OVS metadata/VLAN, OpenFlow matches it → port | **Yes** — createunixsocket must also provision the flow via **rovs** |

So the honest answer: **right now, OSCAL tag routing is not in OpenFlow** — it's reflection at the bridge, so `createunixsocket` stays pure-UDS. If you *want* the subid tag to be the routing key down at the OVS layer, that's a real design change (encode tag → OVS field, emit flows), and then yes, `createunixsocket` would need rovs/OVS.

Which is it — keep reflection-demux (no OVS, finish what I started), or move OSCAL tag routing into OpenFlow (I wire rovs into the create path)?

### 3b. `privacy_provisioner.rs` — step sequence

```
run_provisioning(state, user_id)
  1. load user; if Ready → return (idempotent, FR-8)
  2. mark_provisioning_started (→ Provisioning)
  3. ensure_host_privacy_network()          [from privacy_network.rs]
  4. provision_incus_container(user)        [FR-2]
       retry(3, backoff=[5s,15s,45s])
         incus info ws-<user_id>  OR  incus launch images:debian/12 ws-<user_id>
         wait_for_init(container)
         install_base_packages(container)
  5. inject_wireguard_identity(container, user)   [FR-3]
       incus exec: write privkey + pubkey, chmod 0600
  6. derive_mcp_token(user.wg_public_key) → UUID v5   [FR-3]
  7. seed_mcp_namespaces(container, user, token)  [FR-4]
       POST http://100.90.37.254:3003/mcp  ×  9 keys
  8. if ghostbridge_enabled:
       register_netmaker_peer(user)          [FR-5]  retry(3, backoff)
     else:
       skip
  9. apply_email_privacy_rule(user)          [FR-6]
       if ghostbridge: clear email in CozoDB
  10. publish_user_privacy_route(user, container_name)
  11. publish_openflow_for_privacy_routes()
  12. mark_provisioning_ready(user_id, container, route, token, peer_id)
```

Any step returning `Err` short-circuits to `mark_provisioning_failed`.

### 3c. Incus interaction — no CLI subprocesses in Rust

Per AGENTS.md §4, CLI subprocess calls (`Command::new("incus")`) are **forbidden in plugin
and service code**. The provisioner calls `incus` commands only via an abstraction boundary
defined in `privacy_container.rs`:

```rust
pub trait IncusDriver: Send + Sync {
    async fn container_exists(&self, name: &str) -> Result<bool>;
    async fn launch(&self, image: &str, name: &str) -> Result<()>;
    async fn exec(&self, container: &str, cmd: &[&str]) -> Result<String>;
}
```

The production implementation (`IncusCliDriver`) uses `tokio::process::Command` internally
and is the only place in the codebase that calls the `incus` CLI. Tests inject a mock.
A native OVSDB/REST Incus driver may replace `IncusCliDriver` in a future iteration without
touching provisioner logic.

content.text:
Searched all of `.kiro/specs/`. Here's what's there — and notably what isn't:

**What the specs DO say (`privacy-signup-container-provisioning`):**
- OpenFlow routes are published **per container, keyed by the WG pubkey (identity)** — `publish_openflow_for_privacy_routes()` (design.md:174), and the design explicitly states the pubkey "is used for MCP token derivation, Netmaker registration, **and OpenFlow route publication**" (design.md:208). So the specced role of OpenFlow is **identity/privacy routing** (pubkey-keyed), per container, as a provisioning step.

**What the specs DON'T have — anywhere:**
- **No `container.sock`, no `createunixsocket`, no "shared socket" for containers, no per-container socket demux.** The only "shared socket" hit is `assistant-grpc/design.md` referring to the **D-Bus** bus, unrelated.
- **No OSCAL-subid tag routing in OpenFlow.** Nothing maps a subid tag to an OVS match field.
- `xdp-ovs-incus-network-setup/` is an **empty stub** (no files).

**So the answer to your question:** the specs do **not** put OSCAL tag routing in OpenFlow. They put **identity (pubkey) routing** in OpenFlow — that's the documented OVS role, and it's a provisioning concern, separate from socket creation. The `container.sock` / `createunixsocket` / reflection-demux model isn't specced at all — it lives only in the `unix_socket` plugin's doc/example and this conversation.

**Recommendation grounded in that:** `createunixsocket` stays **pure UDS (reflection-demux), no OVS** — that's consistent with the specs, which reserve OpenFlow for pubkey-identity privacy routing + obfuscation, not socket demux or subid tags. If you want OSCAL-subid tag routing *in* OpenFlow, that'd be **new, unspecced design** — worth a spec of its own before building, rather than bolting OVS onto `createunixsocket`.

Want me to finish `createunixsocket` as pure-UDS reflection-demux (continue what I started), or pause and draft a spec for the OpenFlow-tag-routing idea first?

That's the clean separation, and it matches the compliance model: **the socket is dumb transport; OSCAL is the enforcement/routing layer, separate and flexible.**

- **`container.sock` / `createunixsocket`** = transport only — UDS to tonic-web, reflection demux. It carries OSCAL *subids on its schema* (every mutation is an enforcement point, per your compliance architecture), but it does **not** perform rule-enforcement routing. Dumb pipe.
- **OSCAL rule-enforcement routing** = the separate, "baked-in and very flexible" layer — subid tags driving policy/enforcement decisions (the OpenFlow/gemma side). That's where the flexibility lives, and it's deliberately *not* in the socket.

So the socket stays simple and the OSCAL enforcement-routing is its own thing — good, that's consistent and keeps the socket from becoming a policy chokepoint. So zbusctl should already be able to surface the create — the invocation is just a contract mutation:

```
apply_contract_mutation(plugin_id="unix_socket", value={"sockets":[{"name":"netmaker","path":"/run/ghostbridge/container.sock","ports":[...]}]})
```

So **(b) needs no new code** — it rides the generic plugin-list path. That's the good news.

**(a) is the real gap, and it's specific:** the `unix_socket` plugin's `apply_state` **re-reads `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` and ignores the value passed in** — and `read_desired()` pulls the sockets from the schema's **`example`** field in that SHM catalog. The catalog is written by the projection engine's `write_schemas_to_shm()` from its in-memory schema registry. So `apply_plugin_state` → `apply_state` doesn't persist anything: a mutation never lands in SHM, so the plugin can't see it. That clicks a lot into place: `IncusProxySocket` (`listen: unix:… → connect: tcp:…`) is an Incus **proxy device** — Incus just pipes bytes, treating it as an **HTTP/TCP proxy with no gRPC awareness**. That's incompatible with the tonic-web reflection-demux model, so the right move is to **replace the Incus socket logic in the schema** with the gRPC `container.sock` model.

So the concrete refactor, as I understand it:

- **Deprecate/replace `IncusInstance.sockets: Vec<IncusProxySocket>`** — the per-container `listen→connect` proxy-device representation goes away.
- **Replace it with the gRPC shared-socket model**: the container's schema records its socket as `{ name, ports }` against the single shared `container.sock` (the `SocketEndpoint` I just built in `unix_socket.rs`) — tonic-web demuxes by reflection, no per-container HTTP proxy device.
- **Remove the proxy-device materialization** in the incus plugin's apply (the `config device add … proxy` / `IncusProxySocket` → Incus device path), since Incus is no longer the thing exposing the socket.
- So **"adding a socket updates the container's Incus schema"** = appending the gRPC socket entry (name + ports → shared `container.sock`) to that container's instance, *not* creating an Incus proxy device.

That makes the `unix_socket` plugin (createunixsocket: name/ports/shared socket) the canonical socket model, and the Incus container schema references it instead of carrying its own deprecated proxy-socket logic.

Before I rip out the `IncusProxySocket` proxy-device logic and wire the container schema to the gRPC model — is that the replacement you want (container schema points at the shared `container.sock` via name/ports, Incus stops doing proxy devices entirely)? And should the gRPC socket entry **live on `IncusInstance`** (a field on the container) or stay in the `unix_socket` plugin with the container schema just **referencing it by name**?

content.text:
That's a decisive reason, not just a nicety: the deprecated `IncusProxySocket` is a bare struct with **no `schemars` schema (so nothing to render in the UI) and no D-Bus object (so it's invisible to the D-Bus tree that mirrors the DB)**. The new `unix_socket` `SocketEndpoint` model fixes exactly those gaps — it's schemars-derived (renders, carries OSCAL subids) and rides the plugin's D-Bus host. So the replacement isn't just "gRPC vs HTTP-proxy"; it's "schema'd + D-Bus-exposed vs invisible."

So the settled replacement, pulling all your points together:

- **Deprecate `IncusProxySocket` + the `config device add … proxy` materialization** in `incus.rs` — Incus stops exposing sockets entirely (it only does dumb HTTP/TCP proxy, no gRPC, no schema, no D-Bus).
- **The socket model lives in the `unix_socket` plugin** — `SocketEndpoint { name, path=shared container.sock, ports }` — because that's what gives it the **render schema + OSCAL subids + D-Bus exposure** the Incus version lacked.
- **The container's Incus schema references the socket by `name`** (createunixsocket `--name` = container name); it doesn't carry its own socket struct. "Adding a socket updates the container's schema" = the container now has a named gRPC socket entry resolved through the `unix_socket` plugin, rendered + D-Bus-exposed, instead of an invisible proxy device.

My recommendation: keep the socket in the `unix_socket` plugin (schema'd + exposed), drop `IncusInstance.sockets: Vec<IncusProxySocket>` and its proxy-device apply path, and have the container reference by name — that satisfies "update the container schema," "replace the deprecated incus logic," and "needs render schema + D-Bus exposure" all at once.

Is that the shape you want? If so I'll do the `incus.rs` removal + wire the container→`unix_socket` name reference next. If the socket entry should instead live *on* `IncusInstance` (so a container renders its own sockets directly), tell me and I'll put a schema'd field there instead of a by-name reference.

Both mechanisms exist — and "embedded schema" is the cleaner of the two. Here's what I found:

**Runtime cross-plugin calls do exist** — `full_system.rs` "queries OTHER plugins to build the full state" via D-Bus `Proxy::new`, and `s6.rs` calls the `s6_systemctl` plugin through a typed `S6SystemctlProxy`. So the incus plugin *could* call the unix_socket plugin at runtime. But that's actuation-time coupling — heavier than you need for the schema/rendering.

**Embedded schema is the right fit, and it's basically free.** `SocketEndpoint` is a schemars type — when one struct embeds another, schemars emits the inner as a `$def` and `$ref`s it (your `schema_carries_oscal_subids` test already reads `$defs.SocketEndpoint`, proving it nests). So:

- Define `SocketEndpoint` once in `unix_socket.rs` (done — with OSCAL subids).
- Put **`sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint>` on `IncusInstance`** by importing the type from the unix_socket plugin.
- schemars **embeds** the socket schema into the container schema as a nested `$def` — so the container renders its sockets, the OSCAL subids ride along, and it's exposed on the container's D-Bus object. One source of truth for the socket shape; the unix_socket plugin still owns the binding/reconcile.

That answers "call the plugin in the incus schema" without a runtime call — the container **embeds the unix_socket plugin's schema type** directly, replacing the deprecated, unrendered `IncusProxySocket`.

The one thing to verify when I wire it: the `schemars_adapter` must **resolve the `$ref`** to `SocketEndpoint` into an embedded object when building the `PluginSchema` (otherwise the container schema renders a dangling ref). If it doesn't resolve refs yet, that's the small bit of adapter work this needs.

So the plan: import `SocketEndpoint` into `incus.rs`, replace `sockets: Vec<IncusProxySocket>` with `sockets: Vec<SocketEndpoint>`, delete the proxy-device materialization, and confirm the adapter embeds the `$ref`. Want me to go ahead with that?

**`Instance` adds (read-only):** `name`, `status`, `status_code`, `type`, `project`, `location`, `created_at`, `last_used_at`, `expanded_config` (map), `expanded_devices` (map).

**KEY: Incus has NO first-class "sockets" field.** A proxy socket is just a `devices` entry with `type: proxy`. The op-plugins `incus.rs` `IncusProxySocket` + `sockets: Vec<…>` split is a NON-official invention (and it has no schemars schema / no D-Bus object — invisible to rendering and the mirror). The old struct also carried non-API `image`/`storage_pool` and lacked `expanded_*`/`status_code`/`restore`/`disk_only`.

Decision (2026-06-20): model `devices` as a schemars typed `Device` enum `#[serde(tag="type")]` with all 12 variants; `config` stays a string map (keys too many/dotted to type).

**Socket↔container link = by `name` (foreign key), NOT an embedded field:** `createunixsocket --name <container>` sets `SocketEndpoint.name` = the container `name`; the join happens at the projection/gemma layer (look up container by name + its socket by same name → xray route). Keeps `IncusInstance` faithful to the Incus API; the gRPC `container.sock` stays in the `unix_socket` plugin. See [[project_socket_provisioning]], [[project_cognitive_grpc_endpoint]]. # Incus Proxy Device Configuration Keys

Here are all the configuration keys for the Incus `proxy` device type:

| Key | Type | Required | Purpose |
|-----|------|----------|---------|
| `listen` | string | Yes | "The address and port to bind and listen" |
| `connect` | string | Yes | "The address and port to connect to" |
| `bind` | string | No | Which endpoint to bind on (host or instance; default: host) |
| `nat` | bool | No | Enable NAT-based optimization; requires static instance IP (default: false) |
| `proxy_protocol` | bool | No | "Whether to use the HAProxy PROXY protocol to transmit sender information" (default: false) |
| `uid` | int | No | User ID owning the listening Unix socket (default: 0) |
| `gid` | int | No | Group ID owning the listening Unix socket (default: 0) |
| `mode` | int | No | File mode permissions for the listening Unix socket (default: 0644) |
| `security.uid` | int | No | User ID privilege to drop to (default: 0) |
| `security.gid` | int | No | Group ID privilege to drop to (default: 0) |

The device supports cross-protocol connection types (TCP, UDP, Unix sockets) in non-NAT mode, while NAT mode is limited to TCP and UDP connections.
